Well-designed motivation analysis in Section 2 with quantitative evidence (Fig. 3-4) that ground-truth objects remain accessible in output distributions and vision tokens reveal semantics under vocabulary constraints
Strong reproducibility artifacts: Algorithm 1, detailed hyperparameters, confidence intervals, and extensive case studies with numerical values in appendix
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core components (vocabulary constraint from Li et al. 2023a, JSD selection, element-wise multiplication) are established techniques applied to vision tokens without novel algorithmic contributions or ablations comparing alternative design choices (divergence metrics, combination strategies)

Theoretical claims inadequately supported: (1) vision token projection analysis is somewhat circular—constraining to object categories and finding objects after projection doesn't convincingly establish intrinsic semantic encoding; (2) Table 1 shows grounding doesn't actually hold at hallucinated steps (median ∆=-0.180, p=0.95), contradicting core claims about where vision tokens help

Hyperparameter tuning contradicts 'training-free' positioning: different α per task (10^-5 to 10^-3) and layer selection per architecture (last vs. all layers) require task-specific validation, but no principled selection method provided

strengths: Excellent motivation and analysis: Rigorous investigation of vision tokens (Section 2) with convincing evidence via proper statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank, 95% CIs) that vision tokens encode grounding signals. Figure 3 and 4 compellingly demonstrate the core insight about constrained vocabulary enabling interpretability.

Highly practical method: Training-free with minimal computational overhead (+1.9% vs 2× for competitors), no architectural modifications required. Clever caching of vision token projections demonstrates engineering quality.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation across 5 benchmarks (HallusionBench, CHAIR, POPE, MMMU, VQAv2), 7 model configurations (3 architectures, varying sizes), both generative and discriminative tasks. Strong results on primary benchmarks (HallusionBench qAcc 1.75× improvement).
Thorough ablation studies: Figure 7 systematically ablates key components showing both vocabulary constraint and selection criterion are necessary (full vocab fails with F1=1.52, max-JSD collapses).

Clear and reproducible: Well-structured presentation, detailed supplementary material with confidence intervals, comprehensive implementation details, Algorithm 1 pseudocode, multiple official evaluation protocols followed.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Vocabulary constraint directly from Li et al. (2023a), JSD selection is standard, vision token projection is straightforward. Primary contribution is combination rather than novel components. Key design choices lack principled justification (why JSD? why multiplication in Eq. 6?).

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection: α threshold varies from 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁶ depending on task. Different layer selections for different models (last vs all even layers) without clear principle. Requires task-specific tuning, limiting practical deployability.

Inconsistent and sometimes marginal improvements: CHAIR F1 improvements <1 point in some cases (82.33→83.17). Concerning: CHAIRS metric worsens for LLaVA-1.5-13B (48.0→52.6). MMMU improvements modest (34.39→35.13). POPE mixed across datasets. Statistical significance not always reported.

Analysis gap between motivation and method: Section 2 shows GT objects exist in top-500 but doesn't justify why JSD minimization should recover them. Connection between motivation analysis and actual method design is weak. Limited error analysis of failure cases.

Incomplete design space exploration: Alternative combination rules (multiplication vs averaging/log-space) not compared. Other selection criteria (max-entropy, attention-based) not explored. No oracle experiments or ablations of combination rule (Eq. 6).

Experimental concerns: CHAIR evaluation on 500 images is modest. CODE baseline surprisingly poor (F1=48.50), raising fairness questions. No discussion of model/benchmark interaction effects. Missing oracle upper bounds.
